hints: Compare tests 1 and 2 for W, X, Y and Z. Think about which type of C-Cl bond hydrolyses in cold water and which needs heating with NaOH, and which never releases chloride.
Recall that only one carbonyl type gives a pale yellow precipitate with NaOH plus I2(aq), and only one carbonyl type reduces Fehling's solution to a red precipitate.
Use tests 5 and 6 for Z. Think about what functional group decolourises cold dilute acidified KMnO4, and what combination gives both decolourisation of bromine and a white precipitate.
Link the speed of precipitate with cold AgNO3(aq) to bond strength. Immediate reaction suggests a very easily broken C-Cl bond, very slow suggests a side chain alkyl chloride.
Check that each isomer must still fit molecular formula C8H7ClO with one benzene ring, so count how many extra groups besides the ring are needed for W, X, Y and Z.
walkthrough:
Sort the chlorides using cold silver nitrate**
Think about what test 1 is really doing. $\text{Ag}^{+}(aq) + \text{Cl}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}(s)$ white precipitate only forms if $\text{Cl}^{-}$ is already free in solution. W gives an immediate white precipitate in cold water, so its C-Cl bond must hydrolyse instantly. That is classic for an acyl chloride, $\text{RCOCl} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{RCOOH} + \text{HCl}$. Y gives a precipitate very slowly, so it hydrolyses but much less easily, typical of a primary or secondary alkyl chloride side chain. X and Z give none, so their Cl is not hydrolysed in cold water. That points to aryl chloride, $\text{C-Cl}$ directly on the ring, which is very unreactive.

Confirm with hot sodium hydroxide**
Test 2 boils with $\text{NaOH}(aq)$ which forces hydrolysis of alkyl chlorides as well as acyl chlorides: $\text{RCl} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{ROH} + \text{NaCl}$. After acidification, $\text{AgNO}_{3}$ again detects $\text{Cl}^{-}$. W and Y give white precipitate, confirming hydrolysable Cl. X and Z still give none, confirming their Cl stays bound even on heating. So X and Z must contain aryl chloride.

Pick out the carbonyls with tests 3 and 4**
Test 3 with $\text{NaOH}(aq) + \text{I}_{2}(aq)$ is the triiodomethane test. Only X gives a pale yellow precipitate of $\text{CHI}_{3}$. That proves X contains a methyl ketone group, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO-}$. Test 4 with Fehling's solution warmed gives a red precipitate of $\text{Cu}_{2}\text{O}$ only with an aldehyde. Only Y gives this, so Y contains $\text{-CHO}$. W gives neither, consistent with acyl chloride where the carbonyl carbon is attached to Cl, not to $\text{CH}_{3}$ or $\text{H}$ in a way that gives those tests.

Identify Z as alkene plus phenol**
Only Z decolourises cold, dilute, acidified $\text{KMnO}_{4}(aq)$, so Z contains an easily oxidised $\text{C=C}$ alkene side chain. With $\text{Br}_{2}(aq)$, Z both decolourises and forms a white precipitate. Decolourisation alone means $\text{C=C}$ addition: $\text{C=C} + \text{Br}_{2} \rightarrow \text{CBr-CBr}$. White precipitate with bromine water is diagnostic for phenol, forming 2,4,6-tribromophenol. So Z must contain both alkene and phenol groups, plus the unreactive aryl chloride found in Step 2.

Assemble the group list**
Put it together with the benzene ring already given. W: $\text{COCl}$. X: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}$ and aryl $\text{Cl}$. Y: $\text{CHO}$ and alkyl $\text{RCl}$. Z: $\text{C=C}$, phenolic $\text{OH}$, and aryl $\text{Cl}$. This uses all six test results and keeps each formula at $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{7}\text{ClO}$.

Final answer: W: acyl chloride, $\text{COCl}$
X: methyl ketone, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}$ group and aryl chloride
Y: aldehyde, $\text{CHO}$ and chloroalkane, $\text{RCl}$ (alkyl chloride side chain)
Z: alkene, $\text{C=C}$, phenol, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$, and aryl chloride

hints: Start from formula C8H7ClO with a C6 ring. Count how many carbons are left outside the ring for each isomer and match to the groups found in (a).
For W, think where a COCl unit can fit to give C8. Consider both phenylacetyl chloride and methyl substituted benzoyl chloride forms.
For X and Y, place the Cl and oxygen groups so that X keeps Cl on the ring with a COCH3 group, while Y keeps Cl off the ring with a CHO group.
For Z, build a benzene ring bearing three different substituents OH, Cl and a C2 alkene group to total C8H7ClO.
walkthrough:
Use the carbon count to limit possibilities**
You have $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{7}\text{ClO}$ and a $\text{C}_{6}$ benzene ring in every isomer. That leaves only two carbons outside the ring, unless one substituent is a methyl on the ring plus a one carbon functional group. Keep this in mind as you draw.

Draw W as an acyl chloride**
W must contain $\text{COCl}$. To reach $\text{C}_{8}$, you need either $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COCl}$, phenylacetyl chloride, where the $\text{CH}_{2}\text{COCl}$ side chain provides the extra two carbons, or a ring methyl plus $\text{COCl}$ directly on the ring, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{COCl}$. Both fit the formula and give immediate hydrolysis.

Draw X and Y to fit their carbonyl tests**
X needs aryl Cl plus $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO-}$. The only way to get $\text{C}_{8}$ is $\text{ClC}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{COCH}_{3}$, a chloroacetophenone. The Cl is on the ring, the acetyl group provides the two extra carbons. Y needs alkyl Cl plus $\text{CHO}$. Good fits are $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CHClCHO}$, 2-chloro-2-phenylethanal, where the two side chain carbons carry Cl and CHO, or $\text{OHCC}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$, where CHO is on the ring and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$ is a chloromethyl side chain.

Draw Z as a trisubstituted phenol**
Z needs phenolic OH, aryl Cl and $\text{C=C}$. With only eight carbons total, the ring provides six, so the alkene must be a $\text{C}_{2}$ ethenyl group, $\text{CH=CH}_{2}$. So the structure is a benzene ring with three substituents: $\text{OH}$, $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{CH=CH}_{2}$, written as $\text{HOC}_{6}\text{H}_{3}(\text{Cl})(\text{CH=CH}_{2})$. Any ring positions are acceptable if the groups are correct.

Final answer: W: $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COCl}$ or $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{COCl}$
X: $\text{ClC}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{COCH}_{3}$
Y: $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CHClCHO}$ or $\text{OHCC}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$
Z: $\text{HOC}_{6}\text{H}_{3}(\text{Cl})(\text{CH=CH}_{2})$

hints: Look for a carbon attached to four different groups in your structures for W, X, Y and Z. Focus on the side chain carbon in Y that carries Cl.
walkthrough:
Spot the carbon with four different neighbours**
A chiral centre is a carbon with four different groups and no plane of symmetry. Look at Y as $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CHClCHO}$. The middle carbon is attached to $\text{H}$, to $\text{Cl}$, to $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}$ and to $\text{CHO}$. All four are different, so it is chiral. None of W, X or Z has such a carbon, their side chain carbons have two H atoms or a planar $\text{C=O}$ or $\text{C=C}$. So circle that $\text{CHCl}$ carbon in Y.
Final answer: Circle the chiral carbon in Y: the $\text{CHCl}$ carbon in $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CHClCHO}$, bonded to $\text{H}$, $\text{Cl}$, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}$ and $\text{CHO}$.
